title: UGC NET CS & Applications Grand Mock Test 2024

questions.question_text: Consider a complete bipartite graph K_{m, n}. What is the number of edges and the condition under which K_{m, n} contains an Eulerian circuit?
questions.option_a: m*n edges; Eulerian circuit exists if and only if both m and n are even.
questions.option_b: m+n edges; Eulerian circuit exists if and only if both m and n are odd.
questions.option_c: m*n edges; Eulerian circuit exists if and only if m = n.
questions.option_d: (m*n)/2 edges; Eulerian circuit exists if and only if m is even.
questions.explanation: In K_{m, n}, every vertex in the first partition of size m has degree n, and every vertex in the second partition of size n has degree m. A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit if and only if EVERY vertex has an even degree. Thus, both m (degree of n vertices) and n (degree of m vertices) must be even.
questions.numerical_formula: Eulerian Graph Condition: deg(v) mod 2 == 0 for all v in V. Edges in K_{m, n} = m * n.
questions.common_pitfalls: Confusing Eulerian path (which allows exactly two odd-degree vertices) with Eulerian circuit (requires all even).

questions.question_text: In a 4-stage pipeline with stages S1 (12 ns), S2 (15 ns), S3 (10 ns), and S4 (14 ns), with an interface register delay of 1 ns between consecutive stages, what is the clock period and the speedup achieved for 1000 tasks over non-pipelined execution?
questions.explanation:
Clock cycle time t_clock = max(S1, S2, S3, S4) + register_delay = max(12, 15, 10, 14) + 1 = 15 + 1 = 16 ns.
Total non-pipelined time for 1 task = 12 + 15 + 10 + 14 = 51 ns. For n=1000 tasks, T_non_pipe = 1000 * 51 = 51,000 ns.
Pipelined execution time T_pipe = (k + n - 1) * t_clock = (4 + 1000 - 1) * 16 = 1003 * 16 = 16,048 ns.
Speedup S = T_non_pipe / T_pipe = 51,000 / 16,048 = 3.1779 ~ 3.19.
questions.numerical_formula: Speedup S_n = (n * sum(t_i)) / ((k + n - 1) * (max(t_i) + d_r)). As n -> inf, S -> sum(t_i) / (max(t_i) + d_r).
questions.common_pitfalls: Forgetting to add the 1 ns interface register delay to the bottleneck stage.

questions.question_text: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with functional dependencies: F = { A -> B, B -> C, C -> D, D -> E, E -> F, F -> A }. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.option_a: R has 6 candidate keys and is in BCNF.
questions.option_b: R has only 1 candidate key (A) and is in 3NF but not BCNF.
questions.option_c: R has 6 candidate keys and is in 3NF but not BCNF.
questions.option_d: R has no candidate keys and requires lossy decomposition.
questions.explanation: Since the FDs form a cyclic closure: A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> F -> A, the closure of every single attribute {A}+, {B}+, {C}+, {D}+, {E}+, {F}+ contains all attributes {A, B, C, D, E, F}. Hence each individual attribute is a candidate key (total 6 candidate keys). Since for every FD X -> Y, the determinant X is a superkey, R satisfies the BCNF condition directly.
questions.numerical_formula: BCNF Definition: For every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X must be a superkey of R.
questions.common_pitfalls: Thinking that a relation with multiple candidate keys cannot be in BCNF.

questions.question_text: In Banker's Algorithm for deadlock avoidance, a system has 5 processes (P0 to P4) and 3 resource types (A=10, B=5, C=7). If the Available vector is (3, 3, 2), which condition guarantees the system is in a SAFE state?
questions.option_a: There exists at least one sequence of all processes such that for each process, Need <= Available.
questions.option_b: All resources are currently allocated and none are held by blocked processes.
questions.option_c: Total allocated resources exceed total maximum demands.
questions.option_d: Preemption is enabled across all concurrent threads.
questions.explanation: A state is safe if the system can allocate resources to each process (up to its maximum) in some order and still avoid deadlock. Mathematically, there must exist a safe sequence <P_1, P_2, ..., P_n> such that for each P_i, Need_i <= Available + sum_{j<i} Allocation_j.
questions.numerical_formula: Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] - Allocation[i][j]. Safety check is an O(m * n^2) algorithm.
questions.common_pitfalls: Remember that an unsafe state is NOT necessarily a deadlock; it is merely a state with the potential to deadlock if worst-case requests occur.

questions.question_text: In TCP Congestion Control, if the current Congestion Window (cwnd) is 16 KB and a timeout occurs, what will be the values of the new Slow Start Threshold (ssthresh) and cwnd respectively (assuming Maximum Segment Size MSS = 1 KB)?
questions.explanation: Upon a timeout loss event in TCP Tahoe/Reno: (1) ssthresh is set to half of the current cwnd: ssthresh = max(cwnd/2, 2*MSS) = 16/2 = 8 KB. (2) cwnd collapses back to 1 MSS (1 KB), re-entering the Slow Start exponential growth phase until cwnd >= ssthresh.
questions.numerical_formula: TCP Reno Rule: Timeout => ssthresh = cwnd / 2, cwnd = 1 MSS. (Note: For 3 Duplicate ACKs, Fast Recovery sets cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS).
questions.common_pitfalls: Students frequently confuse the response to a Timeout (cwnd resets to 1) with Triple Duplicate ACK (cwnd halved in Fast Recovery).

questions.question_text: Which of the following problems is DECIDABLE for Context-Free Languages (CFLs)?
questions.option_d: Intersection emptiness (Is L1 intersection L2 = empty?)
questions.explanation: For Context-Free Languages: (1) Membership (w in L): Decidable via CYK algorithm O(n^3). (2) Emptiness (L = empty): Decidable by checking if the start symbol can derive any terminal string. (3) Finiteness: Decidable via cycle detection in reduced CFG. In contrast, Universality, Equivalence, and Intersection-Emptiness are UNDECIDABLE for CFLs.
questions.numerical_formula: Decidability Chart for CFL: Membership (D), Emptiness (D), Finiteness (D), Equivalence (U), Subset (U), Disjointness (U), Universality (U).
questions.common_pitfalls: Assuming that because Equivalence is decidable for Regular languages, it is also decidable for CFLs.

questions.question_text: In heuristic search, an A* search algorithm is guaranteed to return an optimal solution path (admissible) on tree search if the heuristic function h(n) satisfies which condition?
questions.option_a: h(n) <= h*(n) for all nodes n (Underestimation of true cost to goal)
questions.option_b: h(n) >= h*(n) for all nodes n (Overestimation of true cost to goal)
questions.option_d: h(n) is monotonic and strictly decreasing along every path
questions.explanation: An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost to reach the goal: 0 <= h(n) <= h*(n) for all nodes n. For graph search, consistency (monotonicity: h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n')) is additionally required to ensure optimal paths without node re-opening.
questions.numerical_formula: A* Evaluation Function: f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Admissibility: h(n) <= h*(n). Consistency: h(A) <= c(A, B) + h(B).
questions.common_pitfalls: Remember: Overestimating breaks optimality because A* may terminate prematurely on a suboptimal goal.
